history-aqa/elizabethan-england/L01.title: Elizabeth I: background, character and the royal court

anchors.old: Cover this and recall: name three skills or experiences from Elizabeth's upbringing that shaped how she ruled after 1568.
anchors.text: Key Fact Elizabeth’s humanist education (Latin, Greek, theology, rhetoric) and the trauma of imprisonment under Mary I gave her two key tools: the intellectual confidence to argue with ministers and bishops, and the political caution to avoid being trapped by her own decisions.
anchors.new: Explain to a Year 7 in 30 words or fewer how Elizabeth's humanist education and her imprisonment under Mary I each gave her a different tool for ruling.

anchors.old: Close this and explain in one sentence why patronage made an army less necessary for Elizabeth’s control of the country.
anchors.text: Key Fact Patronage tied nobles and gentry to the Crown by reward, not force. Because Elizabeth controlled who got the lands, monopolies and offices, ambitious men had to compete for her favour rather than challenge her authority — provided she kept the rewards flowing.
anchors.new: Apply patronage to a school or club you know: name one reward like Elizabeth's monopolies, lands or offices, and say what happens if the rewards stop flowing.

anchors.text: Why ‘Gloriana’ mattered Elizabeth could not rely on a husband or a strong army to enforce her authority. Instead she used image-making. The Rainbow Portrait shows her with eyes and ears stitched into her robe, suggesting an all-seeing ruler. The Armada Portrait, painted after 1588, places her hand on a globe to imply English mastery of the seas. These were not just decoration — they were political tools shown to ambassadors and copied for nobles to display in their houses.
anchors.new: Sketch the Rainbow and Armada Portraits from memory and label one symbol on each with the message it sent to ambassadors and nobles.

history-aqa/elizabethan-england/L02.title: Key ministers: Cecil, Walsingham and the Privy Council

anchors.old: Cover this and recall the two top offices Cecil held under Elizabeth and the years he served.
anchors.text: Key Fact William Cecil (Lord Burghley) was Principal Secretary 1558–1572 and Lord Treasurer 1572–1598 — almost the entire reign. He was the administrator who turned Elizabeth’s decisions into working policy and prepared his son Robert to succeed him.
anchors.new: Argue for and against: William Cecil, Principal Secretary then Lord Treasurer 1558-1598, was the minister Elizabeth could not do without. Then decide.

anchors.old: Close this and write a one-sentence job description for each of Cecil, Walsingham and the Privy Council.
anchors.text: Key Fact Cecil ran administration and finance; Walsingham ran intelligence and uncovered the Babington Plot of 1586; the Privy Council debated policy and turned the queen’s decisions into instructions sent to officials across the kingdom.
anchors.new: Rank Cecil, Walsingham and the Privy Council by how much each kept Elizabeth safe on her throne, and defend each place in one line.

anchors.text: How Walsingham’s network worked Walsingham paid agents from his own pocket, partly because the Crown was reluctant to fund spies and partly to keep their identities secret from political rivals. His agents posed as Catholic exiles in Paris and Rome, infiltrated seminaries that were training English priests for missions home, and watched the ports for forbidden books. He developed methods for opening, copying and resealing letters without breaking the wax. Code-breakers including Thomas Phelippes worked in his service. None of this had a formal department; it ran through Walsingham’s personal household.
anchors.new: Imagine the Crown paid Walsingham's agents through a formal department, not his personal household. Explain two ways the network would change, for better or worse.

history-aqa/elizabethan-england/L03.title: A female ruler: Parliament, marriage and the succession

anchors.old: Cover this and recall: how often did Elizabeth call Parliament in 45 years, and which two areas did she insist were her prerogative?
anchors.text: Key Fact Elizabeth called Parliament only ten times between 1559 and 1601. She accepted its right to grant taxation and pass laws but ruled that the queen’s marriage and the succession were matters of royal prerogative and not for MPs to debate.
anchors.new: Argue for and against the claim that Elizabeth controlled Parliament, using her ten Parliaments, its right to grant taxation and royal prerogative, then decide.

anchors.old: Close this and write down, from memory, why Elizabeth refused to name her successor and how the succession was settled in 1603.
anchors.text: Key Fact Elizabeth refused to name an heir to avoid creating a focus for plots. After Mary, Queen of Scots, was executed in 1587, Robert Cecil secretly prepared the way for Mary’s Protestant son, James VI of Scotland, who was proclaimed King James I within hours of Elizabeth’s death in March 1603.
anchors.new: Imagine Elizabeth had publicly named James VI as her heir after 1587. Write what might have followed for plotters, Robert Cecil's secret letters and the 1603 succession.

anchors.text: Why Elizabeth treated marriage as a tool, not a goal Elizabeth used marriage negotiations as diplomacy. While Spain and France believed she might still wed their candidate, neither dared invade. Negotiations with the Duke of Anjou in 1581, for example, helped delay open war with Spain by several years. The image of an ‘available’ queen was politically useful even when the reality was that no marriage would happen. Historians treat this deliberate ambiguity as a policy in its own right.
anchors.new: Test this chain: Anjou talks in 1581, Spain and France think Elizabeth may wed, neither invades, war with Spain is delayed. Name the weakest link and explain why.

history-aqa/elizabethan-england/L04.title: Authority at the end of the reign and Essex's rebellion (1601)

anchors.old: Cover this and recall: list three reasons Elizabeth’s authority held in the 1590s despite war, harvests and the deaths of her ministers.
anchors.text: Key Fact Despite the war with Spain, Tyrone’s rebellion in Ireland, four bad harvests (1594–1597) and the deaths of Walsingham (1590) and Burghley (1598), Elizabeth kept her authority through patronage, the Gloriana image, the legacy of 1588, and Robert Cecil’s steady administration.
anchors.new: Sketch scales weighing the war with Spain, Tyrone's rebellion, bad harvests and the deaths of Walsingham and Burghley against patronage, Gloriana, 1588 and Robert Cecil.

anchors.old: Close this and explain in two sentences why Essex’s rebellion collapsed within a single afternoon.
anchors.text: Key Fact Essex’s rebellion failed within hours because Robert Cecil had been warned in advance, declared him a traitor, and got royal heralds onto the streets faster than Essex could rally support. Patronage withdrawn from one ambitious man could not be replaced overnight by armed force.
anchors.new: Find the weakest link in this chain: Cecil warned in advance, Essex declared a traitor, royal heralds on the streets, Essex fails to rally support. Say why.

anchors.text: Why losing the sweet wines monopoly mattered A monopoly on sweet wines meant that Essex could charge a fee on every cask of imported sweet wine sold in England. The income paid for his household, his agents, his soldiers and his political dependents. When Elizabeth let the licence lapse in October 1600, his finances collapsed within months. Several historians, including Penry Williams, see this single decision as the trigger for the rebellion: Essex was not yet ruined, but he believed he soon would be.
anchors.new: Explain to a Year 7, in 30 words or fewer, why Elizabeth letting Essex's sweet wines monopoly lapse in October 1600 could push him towards rebellion.

anchors.old: Cover this box and list Dickens' three key biographical facts: father's imprisonment, childhood work location, and his main goal.
anchors.text: Key Fact Dickens was not born into poverty, but he had direct experience of it. His three key biographical facts for the exam: (1) his father was imprisoned for debt, (2) he worked in a factory as a child, and (3) he wanted to change conditions for the poor, especially children.
anchors.new: Rank Dickens's father's imprisonment for debt, his blacking factory work and his wish to help poor children by how far each drove him to write the novella, a line each.

anchors.old: Cover this box and recall why Dickens chose Christmas as his setting and name three Christmas innovations from the Victorian era.
anchors.text: Key Fact Dickens chose to set his story at Christmas because it was a time when people were already thinking about generosity, family, and goodwill. The Victorian era was when Christmas “went mainstream” — Christmas cards, crackers, and Christmas trees were all introduced during this period. Dickens used the festive season to amplify his message about social responsibility.
anchors.new: Imagine Dickens had set A Christmas Carol in midsummer instead of at Christmas. Write two things his message about social responsibility would lose.

anchors.text: Thomas Malthus & the “Surplus Population” Thomas Malthus was an economist who argued that unchecked population growth would eventually outstrip food and resources, leading to famine and disaster. Some Victorians used his ideas to justify not helping the poor — they believed reducing the population was actually desirable. Dickens despised this attitude. In the novella, Scrooge echoes Malthusian thinking when he says the poor should “decrease the surplus population.” The Ghost of Christmas Present throws these words back at him in Stave 3, forcing Scrooge to confront the cruelty of his own views.
anchors.new: Trace the steps from Thomas Malthus's famine warning to Scrooge's "decrease the surplus population", then name the weakest step in that reasoning and say why.

anchors.old: Cover this box and recall the exact quote Dickens uses to show how Scrooge's internal coldness affects his pointed nose and cheek.
anchors.text: Key Fact Dickens uses pathetic fallacy throughout Stave 1. “The cold within him froze his old features, nipped his pointed nose, shrivelled his cheek.” The cold is not just the weather — it comes from within Scrooge himself. His internal coldness is so powerful that it physically shapes his appearance.
anchors.new: Imagine Dickens wrote that the winter weather froze Scrooge's features. Say what the reader would lose compared with "The cold within him froze his old features".

anchors.old: Cover this box and recall Marley's exact three-word quote about mankind, plus what his chain symbolizes as punishment.
anchors.text: Key Fact Marley tells Scrooge: “Mankind was my business.” This is Dickens’s central message in a single line. Marley’s regret is that he spent his life pursuing wealth when he should have been helping others. The chain he “forged in life” is the punishment for his selfishness — and Scrooge’s chain is even longer.
anchors.new: Write the exam question that Marley's "Mankind was my business" helps answer, then the first sentence of a strong answer that uses the chain he "forged in life".

anchors.text: Scrooge & the Charity Collectors When two charity collectors ask Scrooge for a donation, his response is chilling: “Are there no prisons? And the Union workhouses?” He sees prisons and workhouses as sufficient provision for the poor. When told that many would rather die than go to a workhouse, Scrooge replies that they “had better do it, and decrease the surplus population.” The word “surplus” echoes Malthusian economics and dehumanises the poor, reducing them to a statistic to be managed. Dickens uses this scene to show how wealthy Victorians used economic theory as an excuse to avoid helping those in need.
anchors.new: Link Scrooge's "decrease the surplus population" to the Victorian Context & Dickens' Purpose lesson: say which Victorian attitude Dickens attacks here and how.

anchors.old: Cover this box and recall what springs from the Ghost's head and what this light represents about memories and hidden truths.
anchors.text: Key Fact The Ghost appears with “a bright clear jet of light” springing from its head, representing how memories can illuminate truths about ourselves that we prefer to keep hidden.
anchors.new: Change the end of Stave 2 so Scrooge's cap fully puts out the Ghost's "bright clear jet of light". Write two lines on what that would say about his redemption.

anchors.old: Cover this box and explain what the novella does and does not tell us about Fan's death, and how her loss shapes Scrooge's feelings towards Fred.
anchors.text: Key Fact Fan died young, leaving Fred motherless. Dickens does not reveal the cause of her death, but her loss shapes Scrooge’s complicated feelings towards Fred — he pushes away the last living connection to the sister he loved.
anchors.new: Argue for and against: "Scrooge pushes Fred away because he lost Fan, not because of greed." Give your strongest point each way, then decide.

anchors.text: The Significance of Literary Characters Dickens’ choice of Ali Baba and Robinson Crusoe is significant. Both are stories of isolation and eventual rescue or triumph. This suggests that even as a lonely child, Scrooge had hope and imagination — qualities he has since buried under years of bitterness. The fact that Scrooge weeps when seeing his younger self shows these qualities still exist within him, waiting to be reawakened.
anchors.new: Find the weakest link in this chain: Ali Baba and Robinson Crusoe are tales of isolation and rescue, so young Scrooge had hope, so his weeping proves it survives. Say why.

anchors.old: Cover this box and recall the three symbols of the Ghost of Christmas Present: what does the torch represent, the bare breast, and the empty rusted...
anchors.text: Key Fact The Ghost of Christmas Present symbolises abundance, generosity, and peace. Its torch (cornucopia) represents plenty, its bare breast represents openness and honesty, and its empty, rusted scabbard represents the peace of Christmas. Notice how Scrooge’s attitude has already shifted: he speaks “submissively” and says “if you have aught to teach me, let me profit by it” — a huge change from the man who dismissed Christmas as “humbug.”
anchors.new: Rank the torch, the bare breast and the rusted scabbard by how sharply each contrasts with Scrooge's miserly, closed-off nature, defending each place in a line.

anchors.old: Cover this box and list three phrases showing Scrooge's transformation in Stave 3: his interest in Tiny Tim, his reaction to his own words, and his...
anchors.text: Key Fact Scrooge’s transformation accelerates in Stave 3. He speaks with “an interest he had never felt before” when asking about Tiny Tim. He is “overcome with penitence and grief” when the Ghost throws his own words back at him. He “begged like a boy to be allowed to stay” at Fred’s party. Dickens tracks this change through increasingly emotional language.
anchors.new: Argue for and against the claim that "begged like a boy" shows a bigger change in Scrooge than "overcome with penitence and grief", then decide.

anchors.text: Tiny Tim: Innocence & Suffering Tiny Tim is the emotional heart of the novella. He sits close to his father, who holds his “withered little hand.” The word “withered” suggests premature decay — like a flower that has been deprived of light and nourishment. As a disabled child in a poor family, Tiny Tim has no access to medical care. His catchphrase, “God bless us, every one!” radiates innocence and goodwill despite his suffering. When Scrooge asks the Ghost whether Tiny Tim will live, the Ghost replies using Scrooge’s own words: “If these shadows remain unaltered by the future… the child will die.” Bob’s voice “trembled more when he said that Tiny Tim was growing strong and hearty” — the trembling reveals he does not truly believe his own words. Dickens uses Tiny Tim to put a human face on poverty and to make the consequences of indifference painfully personal for Scrooge.
anchors.new: Imagine Bob's voice did not tremble when he says Tiny Tim is "growing strong and hearty". Write two sentences on what the scene would lose.

anchors.old: Cover this box and recall: What type of cells have DNA in a single loop in cytoplasm, and what extra DNA structures might they contain?
anchors.text: Key Fact Eukaryotic cells (animal and plant) have a nucleus that encloses their DNA. Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) have no true nucleus — their DNA is a single loop in the cytoplasm, and they may also contain plasmids.
anchors.new: Explain to a Year 7, in 30 words or fewer, why a bacterium is prokaryotic but an onion cell is eukaryotic. Use the words nucleus, loop of DNA and plasmid.

anchors.old: Cover this box and recall: Name the three organelles that plant cells have but animal cells don't, and state what bacterial cell walls lack.
anchors.text: Key Fact Plant cells have a cell wall (cellulose), chloroplasts (photosynthesis) and a permanent vacuole (cell sap) in addition to the organelles found in animal cells. Bacterial cells have a cell wall but no chloroplasts, no true nucleus and no mitochondria.
anchors.new: Name the odd one out of animal cell, plant cell and bacterial cell for a cell wall, then again for mitochondria. Say why each time.

anchors.old: Cover this box and recall: Which type of cells differentiate early and permanently, and what tissue allows plants to differentiate throughout life?
anchors.text: Key Fact Most animal cells differentiate early in development and are then permanently specialised. Plant cells can differentiate throughout life because they retain meristem tissue — undifferentiated cells at root and shoot tips.
anchors.new: Suppose plant cells lost their meristem tissue at the root and shoot tips. Say what would happen to a cutting from that plant, and why.

anchors.old: Cover this box and recall: State the max magnification and resolution values for both light microscopes and electron microscopes.
anchors.text: Key Fact Light microscopes: max magnification \(\approx \times 1{,}500\), resolution \(\approx 200\) nm. Electron microscopes: max magnification \(\approx \times 2{,}000{,}000\), resolution \(\approx 0.2\) nm. Higher resolution means finer detail can be distinguished.
anchors.new: Predict whether a light or an electron microscope could show ribosomes. Then check your answer against the 200 nm and 0.2 nm resolution figures.

anchors.old: Cover this box and recall: List the four key steps for this required practical, including coverslip technique and drawing requirements.
anchors.text: Key Fact For this required practical: always start on the lowest power objective, use a stain to make structures visible, lower the coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles, and include a magnification scale on your biological drawing.
anchors.new: Order the slide steps from placing onion epidermis to using the fine focus knob, then pick the step whose skipping would most spoil the image and say why.

anchors.text: Animal Cell Organelles and Their Functions Nucleus — contains the cell’s genetic material (DNA) and controls the cell’s activities. The DNA carries the instructions for making proteins. Cytoplasm — a jelly-like substance where most chemical reactions take place. Enzymes in the cytoplasm control these metabolic reactions. Cell membrane — a thin layer that surrounds the cell and controls which substances enter and leave. It is selectively permeable. Mitochondria — the site of aerobic respiration , where energy is transferred from glucose. Cells that need lots of energy (such as muscle cells) contain more mitochondria. Ribosomes — tiny structures in the cytoplasm where protein synthesis occurs. They are found in both eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells.
anchors.new: Rank nucleus, mitochondria, cell membrane and ribosomes by how badly a muscle cell would cope without each. Defend each place in one line.

anchors.old: Cover this box and recall: how many daughter cells does mitosis produce, what are they genetically, and name the 3 purposes of mitosis.
anchors.text: Key Fact Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells from one parent cell. It is used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction. The cell cycle consists of interphase (growth + DNA replication) followed by mitosis and cell division.
anchors.new: Imagine a cell skips DNA replication in interphase and goes straight into mitosis. Say what each of the two daughter cells would end up with, and why.

anchors.old: Cover this box and recall: define diffusion using 'net movement' and 'concentration', then list all 4 factors affecting diffusion rate.
anchors.text: Key Fact Diffusion is the net movement of particles from high to low concentration. It is a passive process (no energy required). Factors affecting rate: concentration gradient, temperature, surface area and distance.
anchors.new: Predict whether diffusion speeds up or slows down if you raise the temperature, shrink the surface area, then increase the distance, giving the reason for each.

anchors.text: How diffusion, osmosis and active transport move substances across a cell membrane.
anchors.new: Sketch a cell membrane from memory with one arrow each for diffusion, osmosis and active transport, labelling the direction of each and which need energy.

anchors.text: Stem Cells and Their Uses Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that can divide and become specialised. In humans, embryonic stem cells can differentiate into almost any cell type, while adult stem cells (found in bone marrow) are more limited. In plants, meristem tissue retains the ability to differentiate throughout the plant’s life. Stem cells have therapeutic uses — for example, treating paralysis or diabetes — but raise ethical concerns, particularly around the use of embryonic stem cells. You need to be able to discuss both the potential benefits and the ethical objections.
anchors.new: Make the strongest case for and against using embryonic stem cells to treat paralysis or diabetes, then decide which side wins and say why in one line.

anchors.old: Cover this box and write out the complete hierarchy of organisation from cells to organism in the correct order.
anchors.text: Key Fact The hierarchy of organisation: cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism. Each level builds on the one below it.
anchors.new: Link cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism to Cell Structure and Microscopy. Say which level that lesson studied and how it builds the next level.

anchors.old: Cover this box and explain where bile is made, stored, and what two functions it performs in the small intestine.
anchors.text: Key Fact Bile is made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder, and emulsifies fats in the small intestine. It also neutralises stomach acid to create the alkaline conditions needed by intestinal enzymes.
anchors.new: Suppose bile stopped neutralising the hydrochloric acid from the stomach. Use the lock-and-key model to say what would happen to enzymes in the small intestine.

anchors.text: The organs of the human digestive system, from mouth to large intestine.
anchors.new: Sketch the digestive system from memory. Label the stomach, liver, gall bladder, pancreas, small intestine and large intestine with one job each.

anchors.text: The Role of Bile Bile is produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It is released into the small intestine where it has two key functions: it neutralises the hydrochloric acid from the stomach (creating alkaline conditions for enzymes in the small intestine) and it emulsifies fats — breaking large fat droplets into smaller ones to increase the surface area for lipase to work on.
anchors.new: Explain to a Year 7 how bile emulsifying fats helps lipase work, using an everyday comparison, in 30 words or fewer.

science-aqa/biology-paper-1/L04.title: The Heart, Blood and Circulatory Disease

anchors.old: Cover this box. Name the four heart chambers and trace blood flow from vena cava through to aorta in the correct order.
anchors.text: Key Fact The heart has four chambers. Blood flows: vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.
anchors.new: Sketch from memory the route blood takes from the vena cava to the aorta, labelling all four chambers and marking where the blood picks up oxygen.

anchors.old: Cover this box. List the four treatments for coronary heart disease and explain what stents and statins actually do.
anchors.text: Key Fact Coronary heart disease is caused by fatty deposits narrowing the coronary arteries. Treatments include stents (hold arteries open), statins (lower cholesterol), heart transplants and artificial hearts.
anchors.new: Rank stents, statins, heart transplants and artificial hearts from best to worst for a patient with early coronary heart disease, and defend each place in one line.

anchors.text: Coronary Heart Disease Coronary heart disease (CHD) occurs when layers of fatty material (atheroma) build up inside the coronary arteries, reducing blood flow to the heart muscle. This can cause a heart attack if the heart muscle does not receive enough oxygen. Treatments include: stents (wire mesh tubes inserted to hold the artery open), statins (drugs that reduce blood cholesterol levels and slow the build-up of fatty deposits), and in severe cases, heart transplants or artificial hearts (mechanical devices that keep blood flowing while waiting for a transplant).
anchors.new: Write the chain from atheroma building up in the coronary arteries to a heart attack, then mark the link a stent breaks and the link statins break.

anchors.old: Cover this and recall: define natural hazard in one sentence, then list the two main types with one example of each.
anchors.text: Key Fact A natural hazard only becomes a hazard when it threatens people or property. Hazards are split into geological (e.g. earthquakes) and meteorological (e.g. tropical storms).
anchors.new: Choose a natural event near where you live. Decide whether it is a natural hazard or just a phenomenon, and whether it is geological or meteorological.

anchors.old: Close this and write from memory: how do convection currents in the mantle make plates move?
anchors.text: Key Fact Heat from the Earth's core creates convection currents in the mantle. Hot rock rises, cools, and sinks — dragging the plates above it. This is the engine of plate tectonics.
anchors.new: Sketch from memory a labelled diagram linking heat in the core, convection currents in the mantle and the tectonic plates, with arrows showing which way each moves.

anchors.text: Why does the inner core stay solid? The inner core is hotter than the outer core, so logic suggests it should be more molten. But pressure deep inside the Earth is so extreme that atoms cannot move freely — they are forced into a solid lattice. Pressure wins out over heat. This is why seismologists can tell the inner core is solid: certain seismic waves only travel through solids, and they are detected on the far side of the planet only after passing through the inner core.
anchors.new: Suppose the pressure on the inner core fell while its heat stayed the same. Predict what state it would be in, and what seismologists would then detect.

anchors.old: Cover this and write from memory: at a constructive margin, what happens to plates, what is created, and what type of eruption results?
anchors.text: Key Fact At a constructive margin, plates pull apart. Magma rises, cools and forms new crust. Eruptions are gentle and lava flows are runny — Iceland is a key example.
anchors.new: Sketch from memory a cross-section of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge under Iceland, labelling the two plates, rising magma, new crust and runny basalt lava.

anchors.old: Close this and explain in your own words why conservative margins have earthquakes but no volcanoes.
anchors.text: Key Fact Conservative margins slide horizontally past each other. They produce powerful earthquakes (San Andreas Fault) but no volcanoes — nothing is melting in the mantle.
anchors.new: Argue for and against this claim: living by the San Andreas Fault is safer than living by a destructive margin because there are no volcanoes. Then decide.

anchors.text: Why are destructive eruptions so explosive? The descending oceanic plate brings water and trapped gas down with it. As the plate melts in the mantle, this water and gas mixes with the magma and is forced upwards under enormous pressure. By the time it reaches the surface the gas is desperate to escape — the eruption is violent and explosive. Mount St Helens (USA, 1980) is a textbook example: a destructive eruption that blew out the side of a mountain.
anchors.new: Write the chain of steps from a subducting oceanic plate to Mount St Helens in 1980. Circle the one link that makes the eruption explosive instead of gentle.

geography-aqa/paper-1/L03.title: Earthquakes in Contrasting Wealth: Nepal & New Zealand

anchors.old: Cover this and recall: how many people died, how many homes destroyed, and what proportion of GDP was lost in Nepal 2015?
anchors.text: Key Fact Nepal 2015: magnitude 7.8, around 9,000 dead, 600,000 buildings destroyed, 3 million made homeless, $7 billion in damage — roughly a third of Nepal's GDP.
anchors.new: Rank Nepal's 9,000 deaths, 600,000 buildings destroyed, 3 million homeless and $7 billion loss by long-term harm to the country, defending each place in a line.

anchors.old: Close this and write from memory: why did Christchurch (HIC) see far fewer deaths than Nepal (LIC) despite the violent shaking?
anchors.text: Key Fact Christchurch 2011: magnitude 6.3, 185 dead, $40 billion damage. Far lower death toll than Nepal because of strict building codes, fast emergency response, public education and an experienced civil defence service.
anchors.new: Imagine Christchurch kept its fast emergency response and civil defence but had no strict building codes. Say what would follow for the 185 deaths and why.

anchors.text: Why magnitude alone does not predict the death toll Nepal's earthquake was much larger (7.8 vs 6.3 — about 180 times more energy released). Yet its death rate was tens of times higher only partly because of the size. The bigger reason was building quality: brick and mud-mortar construction collapsed; reinforced concrete and timber-frame buildings designed to flex did not. Wealth doesn't change the geology, but it changes everything about how people meet the geology.
anchors.new: Make the case for and against 'Nepal's 7.8 magnitude, not its brick and mud-mortar buildings, caused its death toll', then decide which side wins.

geography-aqa/paper-1/L04.title: Reducing Tectonic Risk: Monitoring, Prediction, Protection, Planning

anchors.old: Cover this and recall: name the three things volcano scientists monitor and what each one tells them.
anchors.text: Key Fact Volcanoes are monitored using seismometers (small tremors signal rising magma), GPS sensors (ground bulges as magma fills the chamber) and gas sniffers (sulphur dioxide rises before an eruption).
anchors.new: Rank seismometers, GPS sensors and gas sniffers by how much you would trust each one alone to warn of an eruption, and defend each place in one line.

anchors.old: Close this and explain in one sentence each: what does each of the four Ps actually do to reduce risk?
anchors.text: Key Fact The four Ps work together. Monitoring gathers data, prediction interprets it, protection makes places stronger, and planning prepares people. Remove any one and the others become weaker.
anchors.new: Link monitoring, prediction, protection and planning as a chain for an earthquake, then name the weakest link and explain how it weakens the others.

anchors.text: Japan's earthquake early-warning system Japan's system doesn't predict earthquakes hours in advance — it gives seconds . Sensors detect the fast-moving but harmless P-waves of a quake, calculate the size, and send alerts to phones, trains and factories before the slower, destructive S-waves arrive. Even ten seconds is enough to stop a bullet train, shut off gas mains and warn people to take cover. It saved hundreds of lives in the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake.
anchors.new: Sketch a timeline from the P-waves arriving to the S-waves arriving, and mark what Japan's early-warning system does in the seconds between.

anchors.old: Without looking, name the three Hebrew terms for the synagogue's three functions — assembly, prayer and study — and write one sentence for each explaining what it means in practice.
anchors.text: Key Fact The synagogue has three functions in Jewish life: beit knesset (house of assembly — community gathering), beit tefillah (house of prayer — worship services), and beit midrash (house of study — Torah learning). Bevis Marks Synagogue in London, established 1701, is the oldest synagogue in continuous use in the United Kingdom.
anchors.new: Rank beit knesset, beit tefillah and beit midrash by how much a small town's Jews would miss each if their synagogue closed. Defend each place in a line.

anchors.old: Name the three main features of the synagogue interior (bimah, aron hakodesh, ner tamid), give the Hebrew meaning of each, and explain what each symbolises.
anchors.text: Key Fact Three essential features: bimah (raised reading platform — centre in Orthodox, front in Reform); aron hakodesh (holy ark — houses Torah scrolls, faces Jerusalem); ner tamid (eternal light — above the ark, never extinguished, symbolises God’s constant presence). The Amidah is the standing prayer recited three times daily at the heart of synagogue worship.
anchors.new: Sketch an Orthodox and a Reform synagogue floor plan side by side. Place the bimah, aron hakodesh and ner tamid in each and label what each one is for.

anchors.text: Further Differences: Dress, Music and the Rabbi's Role Orthodox men cover their heads at all times in the synagogue (and many do so throughout the day); in Reform settings, head covering is encouraged but not always required, and women sometimes choose to wear a kippah. Orthodox services use traditional chazanut (cantorial singing) without musical instruments on Shabbat, as playing instruments is not permitted on the day of rest. Many Reform synagogues use organs or other instruments during services. The rabbi’s role differs too: Orthodox rabbis are always male and serve primarily as legal authorities and preachers; Reform communities have ordained women as rabbis since the 1970s: Sally Priesand was ordained in the United States in 1972, and Jackie Tabick became Britain’s first woman rabbi in 1975.
anchors.new: Argue for and against: the rabbi's role is the biggest Orthodox-Reform difference. Use Jackie Tabick, chazanut and head covering, then decide.

religious-studies-aqa/judaism-practices/.title: Shabbat, Home Worship and Sacred Texts

anchors.old: Without looking, name the five key elements of a traditional Shabbat home observance in order — candle lighting, synagogue, Kiddush, challah, Havdalah — and write one sentence explaining the significance of each.
anchors.text: Key Fact The key elements of Shabbat home observance: candle lighting (Friday at sunset — symbolises the holiness of the day); Kiddush (blessing over wine — sanctifies the day); challah (two braided loaves); synagogue service (Kabbalat Shabbat on Friday evening, Shacharit on Saturday morning); Havdalah (the closing ceremony separating Shabbat from the rest of the week).
anchors.new: Rank candle lighting, Kiddush, challah and Havdalah by how strongly each marks Shabbat as holy, then defend your order in a line each.

anchors.old: Without looking, explain the difference between the Tenakh and the Talmud, name the three sections of the Tenakh, and explain why the Talmud matters for Jewish practice.
anchors.text: Key Fact Tenakh = written law (Torah + Nevi’im + Ketuvim). Talmud = oral law (Mishnah + Gemara). Both are authoritative in Orthodox Judaism; the Talmud shows how Torah principles apply in practice. Reform Jews use both as resources for ethical guidance rather than strictly binding legal codes.
anchors.new: Imagine the Talmud (Mishnah and Gemara) had never existed. Say what problem Orthodox Jews would face in keeping Torah commandments, such as Shabbat, day to day.

anchors.text: Orthodox vs Reform Shabbat Observance Orthodox Jews observe Shabbat strictly, adhering to the traditional 39 prohibitions, walking to synagogue (no driving), and abstaining from electronic devices throughout the day. Reform and Liberal Jews also value Shabbat highly but interpret the prohibitions more individually; many will drive to synagogue if it is far, and some will use electricity for family gatherings or meals. Both traditions affirm that Shabbat is holy and that the day should be set apart from the rest of the week. The difference lies in how that sanctity is expressed: through halakhic restriction (Orthodox) or through personal intention and meaning-making (Reform/Liberal).
anchors.new: Argue for and against the claim that a Reform Jew who drives to synagogue keeps Shabbat less holy than an Orthodox Jew who walks, then decide.

religious-studies-aqa/judaism-practices/.title: Family Life: Birth, Bar and Bat Mitzvah, Marriage and Mourning

anchors.old: Without looking, explain what Bar/Bat Mitzvah marks religiously, describe what happens in an Orthodox ceremony, and explain how this differs in a Reform community.
anchors.text: Key Fact Bar Mitzvah (age 13, boys): called to the Torah in synagogue to read a Hebrew portion; marks religious adulthood and personal responsibility for the mitzvot. Bat Mitzvah (age 12, girls): Reform and Liberal girls read from the Torah on equal terms; in Orthodox communities the ceremony takes a different form. Both mark the transition from childhood religious life to full adult religious responsibility.
anchors.new: Say what would change if a girl moved from an Orthodox to a Reform synagogue before her Bat Mitzvah at 12, and what the Bat Mitzvah would still mean for her.

anchors.old: Name the four life-cycle ceremonies in this lesson (Brit Milah, Bar/Bat Mitzvah, wedding, shiva/kaddish) and for each write one sentence explaining its religious significance.
anchors.text: Key Fact Four key Jewish life-cycle ceremonies: Brit Milah (8th day — sign of the covenant with Abraham); Bar/Bat Mitzvah (13/12 years — religious adulthood, responsibility for the mitzvot); Wedding (chuppah — God’s presence; ketubah — shared obligations; breaking the glass — memory amid joy); Shiva (7-day mourning at home) and Kaddish (11 months of praise to God in grief).
anchors.new: Rank Brit Milah, Bar/Bat Mitzvah, the wedding, and shiva with kaddish by how much each needs the community present. Defend each place in a line.

anchors.text: The Breaking of the Glass: Memory and Joy The breaking of the glass at the end of a Jewish wedding is one of the most distinctive and widely observed traditions. It recalls the destruction of the First and Second Temples in Jerusalem — a defining trauma in Jewish history — and reminds the assembled guests that even in the greatest happiness, Jews do not forget the losses of their people. The Talmud records that a great sage broke a glass at his son’s wedding when he felt the rejoicing was becoming excessive. Today, the shout of “Mazel tov!” (“Good fortune!”) immediately follows the breaking, balancing memory with celebration.
anchors.new: Argue for and against: breaking the glass for the destroyed Temples spoils the joy of a wedding. Use the Talmud's sage and “Mazel tov”, then decide.

anchors.old: Without looking, name the three key rules of kashrut — permitted animals, kosher slaughter and milk/meat separation — and for each give the Torah reference or principle behind it.
anchors.text: Key Fact Three rules of kashrut: (1) Permitted animals only (chew cud + split hooves for land animals; fins + scales for fish) — Leviticus 11. (2) Kosher slaughter (shechita) minimising suffering — draining of blood because “the life of the flesh is in the blood” (Leviticus 17:11). (3) Separation of milk and meat — Exodus 23:19 (“Do not cook a young goat in its mother’s milk”).
anchors.new: Rank the three kashrut rules (permitted animals, shechita, separating milk and meat) by how hard each is to keep in a British school canteen, one line each.

anchors.old: Name the three festivals covered in this lesson, give the Hebrew name for each, write one sentence on what each commemorates and one sentence on a key observance.
anchors.text: Key Fact Rosh Hashanah : Jewish New Year; shofar, reflection, Book of Life, Ten Days of Awe begin. Yom Kippur : Day of Atonement; 25-hour fast, Vidui (confession), teshuvah (repentance). Pesach : Passover; Exodus from Egypt; matzah replaces all leavened bread; the Seder retells the Exodus with symbolic foods.
anchors.new: Name the odd one out of Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and Pesach, then justify it using what each festival remembers or asks of Jews.

anchors.text: Different Jewish Views on Dietary Laws Orthodox Judaism observes the full requirements of kashrut strictly, including separation of milk and meat, kosher slaughter, and the avoidance of all non-kosher animals and their products. Kashrut is understood as a divine mitzvah binding on all Jews regardless of their personal understanding of its reason. Reform Judaism approaches kashrut with greater personal autonomy. Reform communities teach the value and meaning of kashrut — its connection to Jewish identity, the care it encourages in eating, and the discipline it builds — but many Reform Jews choose how much of kashrut to observe based on personal conviction rather than strict halakhic requirement. Some observe full kashrut; others keep a partial form (e.g. avoiding pork and shellfish) or none at all. Liberal Judaism similarly emphasises personal decision and intention over strict legal obligation. The Board of Deputies of British Jews, which represents a wide range of British Jewish communities, includes communities across all these positions. This diversity of practice is real and important — when the exam asks about “different Jewish views,” the distinction between Orthodox, Reform and Liberal practice on kashrut is precisely what is expected.
anchors.new: Make the strongest case for the Orthodox view that kashrut is a mitzvah binding all Jews, then for Reform personal autonomy, then decide which convinces you.

anchors.old: Cover this and list the three internal sources of finance from memory, with one sentence on each.
anchors.text: Key Fact Internal sources — retained profit, selling unwanted assets, owner’s savings — do not involve borrowing or outside investors. They cost nothing in interest, but the business has to already have the money or the asset to use them.
anchors.new: Choose a local shop you know and decide which internal source (retained profit, selling unwanted assets or owner's savings) could fund a new till, and why the others would not.

anchors.old: Close this and name three external sources only available to Ltds and plcs, not sole traders.
anchors.text: Key Fact New share issues are only available to limited companies (Ltd and plc). Sole traders and partnerships cannot sell shares — they rely on savings, retained profit, loans, overdrafts and trade credit instead.
anchors.new: Imagine Tesco were a sole trader, not a plc. Say which source of finance it would lose, and which sources it would have to rely on instead.

anchors.text: The Three Internal Sources Retained profit — profit the business has made and kept back rather than paid out to owners. It is free: no interest, no repayment, no loss of control. The downside is that a new business has no profit yet, and using retained profit means the owners receive less income this year. Selling unwanted assets — a business sells off spare machinery, an old van, or a property it no longer uses. This frees up cash quickly, but only works if the business actually owns something worth selling, and the asset cannot be recovered if the business needs it later. Owner’s savings — the entrepreneur puts personal money into the business. Cheap and quick, but risky for the owner: if the business fails they lose their savings as well as their income.
anchors.new: Rank retained profit, selling unwanted assets and owner's savings from least to most risky for the owner, and defend each place in one line.

anchors.old: Cover this and explain, in one sentence, why a profitable business can still run out of cash.
anchors.text: Key Fact Profit is not the same as cash. A business can be profitable and still fail if cash is not available to pay wages, rent and suppliers on the day they are due. Cash is about timing; profit is about the full trading year.
anchors.new: Imagine a business selling on 90-day trade credit doubles its sales in one month. Say what happens to its profit and to its cash that month, and why.

anchors.old: Close this and write, from memory, the two-step calculation for a closing balance given opening balance, inflows and outflows.
anchors.text: Key Fact Closing balance = Opening balance + Net cash flow. Net cash flow = Cash inflows − Cash outflows. The closing balance of one month is the opening balance of the next.
anchors.new: Predict the Newquay surf shop's closing balance at the end of February if it repeats January's £12,000 in and £15,000 out, then check it against the lesson.

anchors.text: The Four Rows of a Cash-Flow Forecast Cash inflows — money coming in from sales, loans, investment or asset sales. Cash outflows — money going out on wages, rent, stock, utilities, loan repayments. Net cash flow — inflows minus outflows for that month. It can be positive or negative. \(\text{Net cash flow} = \text{Total inflows} - \text{Total outflows}\) Opening and closing balances — the opening balance is how much cash the business had at the start of the month. The closing balance is opening balance + net cash flow, and it becomes the next month’s opening balance.
anchors.new: Choose a business you know, list two cash inflows and three cash outflows for its cash-flow forecast, then say which month its net cash flow might turn negative and why.

anchors.old: Cover this and write down, from memory, one example each of a fixed cost and a variable cost for a UK coffee shop.
anchors.text: Key Fact Fixed costs stay the same when output changes (rent, salaries, insurance). Variable costs change directly with output (raw materials, packaging, hourly wages). Total costs = fixed + variable.
anchors.new: Choose a business you know, list two of its fixed costs and two variable costs, and say which of the four would double if its sales doubled.

anchors.old: Close this and recall the three formulae: total costs, revenue and profit. Write them out without peeking.
anchors.text: Key Fact The three core formulae: Total costs = Fixed + Variable. Revenue = Price × Quantity sold. Profit = Revenue − Total costs. Every AQA Finance calculation is built from these three.
anchors.new: Draw a flow chart that starts with Fixed costs, Variable costs, Price and Quantity sold and ends at Profit, labelling the formula at each join.

anchors.text: Why the Fixed/Variable Split Matters High fixed costs, low variable costs — think of a cinema. The building, projector and staff salaries are expensive, but each extra viewer costs almost nothing. Once fixed costs are covered, every extra ticket sold is nearly pure profit. But if attendance drops, the huge fixed costs still have to be paid. Low fixed costs, high variable costs — think of a market-stall sandwich seller. Stall rent is low, but bread, fillings and packaging cost real money per sandwich. Profit per unit is smaller but the business is far less risky in a quiet week.
anchors.new: Argue for and against the claim that a cinema is riskier than a market-stall sandwich seller, using fixed and variable costs, then decide.

anchors.old: Cover this and write the break-even formula from memory, then explain what contribution per unit means in one sentence.
anchors.text: Key Fact Break-even (units) = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Contribution = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Every unit sold above the break-even point adds its contribution to profit.
anchors.new: Choose a business you know, invent a selling price, variable cost per unit and fixed costs, then work out its contribution per unit and break-even in units.

anchors.old: Close this and write the ARR formula from memory. Then list the two things ARR does NOT take into account.
anchors.text: Key Fact ARR = (Total profit ÷ years) ÷ Initial investment × 100. It gives the average annual return as a percentage. It does NOT take timing of returns or the risk of the project into account — these have to be considered separately.
anchors.new: Argue for and against the claim that the project with the higher ARR is always the better choice, using timing of returns and risk, then decide.

anchors.text: What Happens When Variables Change If fixed costs rise — say rent increases by £300 a week — the break-even point rises because the numerator in the formula is bigger. Oakleaf would now need to sell £1,500 ÷ £2.40 = 625 lattes per week, not 500. If selling price rises — say the latte goes up to £4.00 — contribution becomes £4.00 − £1.10 = £2.90. Break-even falls to £1,200 ÷ £2.90 = 414 lattes. The shop has to sell fewer units because each one contributes more. If variable costs rise — say milk prices go up, pushing variable cost to £1.40 — contribution falls to £2.10. Break-even rises to £1,200 ÷ £2.10 = 572 lattes.
anchors.new: Cover the figures, then predict whether Oakleaf's break-even rises or falls when rent goes up £300, the latte goes to £4.00 and variable cost goes to £1.40.

anchors.old: Cover this and write out the 8 place values from memory, then use them to convert 10110100 to denary.
anchors.text: Key Fact An 8-bit binary number has place values 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 (left to right). To convert binary to denary, add up the place values where the digit is 1. The maximum 8-bit value is 11111111 = 255. Decimal values from 0 to 255 must be representable.
anchors.new: Imagine 11111111 gains a ninth bit on the left. Write that bit's place value and the new maximum, then explain why 255 was the limit with 8 bits.

anchors.old: Test yourself: convert 10110011 to hex without notes. Split into nibbles, convert each, write the two hex digits.
anchors.text: Key Fact To convert binary to hex: split into groups of 4 bits (nibbles) from the right, then convert each nibble to its hex digit. The maximum 8-bit value is FF in hex, 255 in denary. To convert hex to denary: multiply the first digit by 16 and add the second.
anchors.new: Predict which is biggest: FF, 11111111 or 255. Then check by splitting 11111111 into nibbles and using the multiply-by-16 rule on FF.

anchors.text: Worked Example — Converting Between Binary and Denary Binary → Denary: Convert 10110010 Write out place values and match each bit: 128: 1 → 128 64: 0 → 0 32: 1 → 32 16: 1 → 16 8: 0 → 0 4: 0 → 0 2: 1 → 2 1: 0 → 0 Total: 128 + 32 + 16 + 2 = 178 Denary → Binary: Convert 157 128 fits: 157 − 128 = 29, write 1 64 does not fit in 29, write 0 32 does not fit in 29, write 0 16 fits: 29 − 16 = 13, write 1 8 fits: 13 − 8 = 5, write 1 4 fits: 5 − 4 = 1, write 1 2 does not fit in 1, write 0 1 fits: 1 − 1 = 0, write 1 Result: 10011101
anchors.new: Find the step in converting 157 to 10011101 where a pupil is most likely to slip, and write the wrong binary answer that slip would produce.

anchors.old: Cover this and recall: what ASCII code is 'A'? What is 'a'? What is '0'? Now calculate the code for 'F' and for 'n'.
anchors.text: Key Fact In ASCII: upper-case A = 65, lower-case a = 97, digit 0 = 48. Because codes are sequential within each group, you can calculate any character’s code: ‘F’ = 65 + 5 = 70 . ‘n’ = 97 + 13 = 110 . ASCII uses 7 bits and covers 128 characters (0–127).
anchors.new: Convert A = 65, a = 97 and 0 = 48 into 7-bit binary using Number Bases, then explain why 7 bits limits ASCII to 128 characters.

anchors.old: Test yourself: name two advantages of Unicode over ASCII, and explain what backwards-compatibility with ASCII means in practice.
anchors.text: Key Fact Unicode uses the same codes as ASCII for characters 0–127, but extends far beyond to cover every writing system in use worldwide. This backwards-compatibility means ASCII files are readable by any Unicode system without conversion. Unicode can represent over one million characters; ASCII can only represent 128.
anchors.new: Make the strongest case for and against this claim: Unicode keeping ASCII's codes 0–127 mattered more than reaching over one million characters. Then decide.

anchors.text: Worked Example — Character Code Calculations Example 1: Given that A = 65, what is the code for G? G is the 7th letter (A=1, B=2, C=3, D=4, E=5, F=6, G=7). G = 65 + (7 − 1) = 65 + 6 = 71 Example 2: A character has the ASCII code 100. What character is it? Lower-case a = 97. 100 − 97 = 3. Count 3 letters on from a: b, c, d . The character is ‘d’. Example 3: Given that digit 0 = 48, what code represents the character ‘7’? 7 is 7 positions after 0: 48 + 7 = 55 . Note: ‘7’ as a character (code 55) is different from the integer 7 (the value itself). This distinction matters when sorting or comparing strings.
anchors.new: Predict the order a computer sorts '7', 'G', 'd' and 'a', then check it by working out each ASCII code from A = 65, a = 97 and 0 = 48.

anchors.old: Cover this and write the formula for image file size in bits, then convert your answer to bytes. Then check.
anchors.text: Key Fact Image file size (bits) = W × H × D, where W is width in pixels, H is height in pixels, and D is colour depth in bits. To convert to bytes, divide by 8.
anchors.new: Work out what happens to an image's file size if its width and height both double but its colour depth halves, using W × H × D, and explain why.

anchors.old: Test yourself: a 4-bit colour depth gives how many possible colours? Write your calculation.
anchors.text: Key Fact The number of colours available at a given colour depth = 2 depth . So 4-bit = 2 4 = 16 colours; 8-bit = 2 8 = 256 colours; 24-bit = 2 24 = 16,777,216 colours. Doubling the bit depth squares the number of available colours.
anchors.new: Predict how many colours a 16-bit colour depth gives using 2 to the power of depth, then check it against the rule that doubling the bit depth squares the colours.

anchors.old: Cover this. Write out the sound file size formula from memory, then use it: rate 44,100 Hz, resolution 16 bits, duration 10 seconds.
anchors.text: Key Fact Sound file size (bits) = sampling rate × sample resolution × duration (seconds). To convert to bytes, divide by 8. Always check which unit the question asks for.
anchors.new: Pick a song you know, estimate its length in seconds, then work out its mono file size in bytes at a 44,100 Hz sampling rate and 16-bit sample resolution.

anchors.text: Worked Example: Calculating Image File Size Problem: A bitmap image is 800 pixels wide and 600 pixels tall. It uses a colour depth of 24 bits per pixel. Calculate the file size in megabytes. Step 1 — Apply the formula: Size (bits) = W × H × D = 800 × 600 × 24 = 11,520,000 bits. Step 2 — Convert to bytes: 11,520,000 ÷ 8 = 1,440,000 bytes. Step 3 — Convert to megabytes (using SI prefix: 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes): 1,440,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 1.44 MB. Common mistake: Forgetting to divide by 8. The formula gives bits — always convert to bytes for the final answer unless the question specifies bits.
anchors.new: Find the step most likely to be dropped in the 800 × 600 × 24 worked example, then work out the wrong megabyte answer a pupil would get without it.

computer-science-aqa/data-representation.title: Data Compression: Huffman and Run-Length Encoding

anchors.old: Cover this and recall: what is lossless compression and how does it differ from a method that permanently removes data?
anchors.text: Key Fact Lossless compression reduces file size without losing any data. The original file can be perfectly reconstructed. This is essential whenever data integrity matters — for example, text files, program code, medical images and database backups.
anchors.new: Rank text files, program code, medical images and database backups by how much harm losing data would cause if compressed lossily, defending each place in one line.

anchors.old: Close this and write out the three steps for calculating bits saved by Huffman coding. Check you included: ASCII total, Huffman total, subtraction.
anchors.text: Key Fact Bits saved = (number of characters × 7) − (sum of frequency × code length for each character). Always show both totals before subtracting. Set out each step clearly so your method can be followed.
anchors.new: Write out the three steps of the bits-saved method for a 10-character message, then say which step, if left out, would make the method hardest to follow.

anchors.text: Interpreting a Huffman Tree — Worked Example Suppose a Huffman tree is given for four characters. Reading left as 0 and right as 1: Character E (most frequent) — at depth 1 — code: 0 (1 bit). Character T (second most frequent) — at depth 2 — code: 10 (2 bits). Character A — at depth 3 — code: 110 (3 bits). Character Z (least frequent) — at depth 3 — code: 111 (3 bits). To encode the string “EETA”: E=0, E=0, T=10, A=110 → 0 0 10 110 = 7 bits total (1 + 1 + 2 + 3). In standard 7-bit ASCII, “EETA” would need 4 × 7 = 28 bits. Huffman encoding saves 21 bits for this short string. Important: In your exam you will always be given the Huffman tree. You are not required to construct a tree from scratch — only to read codes from a given tree and calculate the total bits saved.
anchors.new: Make up a five-letter string using only E, T, A and Z, encode it with the tree's codes, then work out how many bits it saves against 7-bit ASCII.

anchors.old: Cover this and write down the three processes of memory in order, with a one-sentence description of each.
anchors.text: Key Fact Memory works through three processes: encoding (converting input into a storable form), storage (holding the information), and retrieval (getting the information back out). Without all three, a memory cannot be used.
anchors.new: Think of something you forgot this week, then decide whether encoding, storage or retrieval was the weak link and give one reason for your choice.

anchors.old: Close this and write one example from your own life for each of the three types of long-term memory: episodic, semantic, procedural.
anchors.text: Key Fact The three types of long-term memory are: episodic (personal events tied to a time and place), semantic (general knowledge and facts), and procedural (how to perform learned skills). Procedural memory operates largely without conscious recall.
anchors.new: Choose a sport or hobby you do and write one example from it of episodic memory, one of semantic memory and one of procedural memory.

anchors.text: Why Retrieval Can Fail Retrieval failure happens when information has been stored but cannot be accessed at that moment. This can occur because the right retrieval cue is missing — a trigger such as a context, smell, or related word that helps unlock the memory. Without the cue, the memory stays out of reach. Retrieval failures can also happen when competing memories interfere with each other, a process called interference that is covered in detail in a later lesson.
anchors.new: Predict whether you would recall your first day at secondary school better standing in the school or sitting at home, and explain why using retrieval cues.

anchors.old: Cover this and draw the three stores as boxes. In each box, write the coding, capacity and duration from memory.
anchors.text: Key Fact The multi-store model has three stores: the sensory register (large capacity, very brief duration), short-term memory (limited capacity of about 7 items, up to about 30 seconds), and long-term memory (potentially unlimited capacity, potentially permanent duration).
anchors.new: Pick the odd one out of the sensory register, short-term memory and long-term memory, first by capacity, then by duration, and say why each time.

anchors.old: Test yourself: write the coding, capacity and duration for STM and LTM side by side without looking at this page.
anchors.text: Key Fact STM codes mainly acoustically, holds about 7 items (±2), and lasts up to around 30 seconds without rehearsal. LTM codes mainly semantically, has potentially unlimited capacity, and can last a lifetime.
anchors.new: Pick a phone number you know by heart and one you saw only once. Use acoustic and semantic coding and STM's 7 ±2 limit to explain why only one stuck.

anchors.text: Peterson & Peterson (1959): Evidence for STM Duration Peterson & Peterson (1959) is the AQA named study for STM duration. Aim — to investigate the duration of STM without rehearsal. Method — participants were given a consonant trigram (e.g. CHJ) and immediately required to count backwards in threes from a given number to prevent rehearsal; recall was tested after intervals of 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 or 18 seconds. Results — recall fell sharply with time; after 18 seconds, recall dropped to approximately 5% of items. Conclusion — without rehearsal, STM duration is approximately 18–30 seconds.
anchors.new: Imagine Peterson & Peterson's participants had not counted backwards in threes. Say how recall of the trigram at 18 seconds would change from about 5%, and why.

anchors.old: Cover this and explain why the primacy effect and the recency effect each occur, linking each to a different memory store.
anchors.text: Key Fact The primacy effect refers to better recall of items at the start of a list; the recency effect refers to better recall of items at the end. The primacy effect is explained by transfer to long-term memory via rehearsal; the recency effect is explained by items still being active in short-term memory.
anchors.new: Predict what happens to the primacy effect and the recency effect if people do a distracting task before recall, then explain each using STM and LTM.

anchors.old: Cover this and write Murdock's aim, method, results and conclusion from memory in four bullet points.
anchors.text: Key Fact Murdock (1962): Aim — to investigate the serial position effect in free recall. Method — participants heard lists of words (typically 20 words, presented at a rate of one word per second) and were asked to recall them in any order immediately afterwards. Results — words at the start (primacy) and end (recency) were recalled better than words in the middle; a U-shaped serial position curve was produced. Conclusion — the pattern supports the idea of separate STM and LTM stores.
anchors.new: Change Murdock's method so participants do a distracting task before recalling the 20 words. Say what happens to primacy and recency, and why.

anchors.text: The Serial Position Curve When psychologists plot the probability of recall against the position of each word in a list, the result is a U-shaped graph called the serial position curve . Recall is high for the first few words (primacy), drops in the middle, and rises again for the last few words (recency). This characteristic shape appears consistently across many free recall studies.
anchors.new: Sketch the serial position curve from memory, label both axes, primacy and recency, and note beside each end which store those words are recalled from.

anchors.old: Cover this and explain in your own words what 'effort after meaning' means and why it causes memory errors.
anchors.text: Key Fact Bartlett’s Theory of Reconstructive Memory proposes that recall is an active reconstruction shaped by schemas and the effort after meaning. This explains why our recollections often change over time, filling in gaps to match what we expect rather than what actually occurred.
anchors.new: Choose a story you heard second-hand, such as a school rumour, and explain how schemas and effort after meaning could change it in each retelling.

anchors.old: Write Bartlett's War of the Ghosts: aim, method, results, conclusion from memory as four brief bullet points.
anchors.text: Key Fact Bartlett’s War of the Ghosts study: Aim — to investigate how memory for an unfamiliar story changes over time. Method — British participants read the story and recalled it repeatedly over intervals ranging from hours to years. Results — participants altered, shortened and rationalised the story to fit familiar cultural expectations; unfamiliar elements were omitted or replaced. Conclusion — memory is an active reconstruction shaped by prior knowledge and schemas, not a faithful replay.
anchors.new: Imagine Bartlett had given his British participants a familiar British folk tale instead of The War of the Ghosts. Say what would follow for his results and conclusion.

anchors.text: Evaluating Bartlett’s Study A strength of Bartlett’s study is its ecological validity — participants recalled a meaningful story rather than an artificial list of words, which is closer to real-world memory tasks. The repeated recall method also reveals how memory changes over time, which has practical implications for eyewitness testimony. A weakness is that Bartlett’s methods were not tightly controlled. The story was not standardised in all versions, and Bartlett did not use statistical analysis — he relied on qualitative descriptions of changes. This makes it harder to replicate precisely and limits how confidently we can draw general conclusions from his data.
anchors.new: Make the strongest case for and against the claim that the War of the Ghosts study is too loosely controlled to trust, then decide which side wins.

anchors.old: Cover this and name the bones at the shoulder, elbow, hip, knee and ankle from memory. Then state what type of joint is found at the shoulder and hip.
anchors.text: Key Fact Ball-and-socket joints are found at the hip (pelvis and femur) and shoulder (scapula and humerus). Hinge joints are found at the elbow (humerus, radius, ulna), knee (femur and tibia) and ankle (tibia, fibula and talus).
anchors.new: Pick a sport you play. Name one action using a ball-and-socket joint (hip or shoulder) and one using a hinge joint (elbow, knee or ankle), with the bones at each.

anchors.old: Write the six functions of the skeleton from memory and then apply each one to a named sporting example.
anchors.text: Key Fact The six functions of the skeleton are: support, protection, movement, attachment for muscles, mineral storage and blood cell production. Each one can be applied to sport — for example, the femur acts as a lever during kicking (movement) and the ribs protect the lungs during a tackle (protection).
anchors.new: Rank support, protection, mineral storage and blood cell production by how much they matter to a rugby player during a match, and defend each place in a line.

anchors.text: Bone Types and the Movement They Allow The spec distinguishes between long bones and short bones in terms of movement. Long bones such as the femur, tibia, humerus, radius and ulna enable gross movements — the large, powerful movements used in sprinting, jumping and throwing. Short bones, such as those in the wrist and ankle, enable finer, more controlled movements. Flat bones such as the cranium, ribs and scapula serve a protective function and provide broad surfaces for muscle attachment. The shape and design of each bone directly determines how much movement it allows. The rounded head of the femur fits into the cup-shaped socket of the pelvis, allowing movement in all directions at the hip. The pulley-shaped end of the humerus fits into the groove of the ulna at the elbow, restricting movement to a single plane (flexion and extension only).
anchors.new: Imagine the end of the humerus were rounded like the head of the femur, not pulley-shaped. Say what would change at the elbow during a bicep curl.

anchors.old: Without looking, name the agonist and antagonist during: (1) elbow flexion in a bicep curl, (2) knee extension in kicking, (3) plantar flexion in a sprinting push-off.
anchors.text: Key Fact In a bicep curl upward phase: biceps = agonist (concentric contraction), triceps = antagonist. In kicking (knee extension): quadriceps = agonist, hamstrings = antagonist. In a sprinting push-off (plantar flexion): gastrocnemius = agonist, tibialis anterior = antagonist.
anchors.new: Swap the sprinting push-off for pulling the toes upwards. Say what happens to the roles of gastrocnemius and tibialis anterior, and name the new movement.

anchors.old: Close this and describe the type of contraction happening in each phase: (1) bicep curl upward, (2) bicep curl downward, (3) gymnast holding a handstand.
anchors.text: Key Fact Concentric = muscle shortens (produces movement). Eccentric = muscle lengthens under tension (controls or brakes movement). Isometric = muscle produces tension but no joint movement occurs. All three can happen in the same exercise: a squat involves concentric quadriceps on the way up, eccentric on the way down, and isometric if you pause at the bottom.
anchors.new: Choose a movement from a sport you play. Find a concentric, an eccentric and an isometric contraction in it, and name the muscle working each time.

anchors.text: Misconception: naming one muscle without its partner A very common error in exams is to name a single muscle as ‘the agonist’ without specifying the joint, the direction of movement, or the antagonist. A full answer names the agonist, names the antagonist and describes the action at the correct joint. Writing ‘the biceps is the agonist’ alone will not earn full marks. Always frame answers as: “During elbow flexion, the biceps acts as the agonist (prime mover) while the triceps acts as the antagonist at the elbow joint.”
anchors.new: Write a 3-mark question on the antagonistic pair at the ankle when jumping, then a first sentence of an answer naming joint, movement, agonist and antagonist.

physical-education-aqa/human-body-and-mo.title: Synovial Joints and Types of Movement

anchors.old: Cover this and recall the six structures of a synovial joint, writing what each one does to prevent injury.
anchors.text: Key Fact The six key structures of a synovial joint are: synovial membrane (produces fluid), synovial fluid (reduces friction), joint capsule (encloses and seals the joint), bursae (cushion tendons against bone), cartilage (absorbs compression and provides frictionless surface), and ligaments (connect bone to bone for stability).
anchors.new: Imagine the synovial membrane in a runner's knee stopped working. Trace what would happen next to the synovial fluid, then to the articular cartilage.

anchors.old: Close this and list every type of movement available at the shoulder. Then list the movements available at the knee. Compare the two to explain why joint type matters.
anchors.text: Key Fact Shoulder (ball-and-socket): flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation, circumduction. Knee (hinge): flexion and extension only. Ankle (hinge): plantar flexion and dorsiflexion only. The more movements a joint allows, the greater the sporting versatility — but often at the cost of stability.
anchors.new: Argue for and against: the shoulder suits sport better than the knee because it allows rotation and circumduction. Weigh in stability, then decide.

anchors.text: Applying joint structures to injury prevention A 4-mark exam question might ask how the structures of a synovial joint help prevent injury during sport. A well-developed answer links each structure to its protective role: ligaments prevent bones from moving too far out of alignment (stabilising the knee in a tackle); bursae prevent tendons from rubbing on bone during repeated movements (protecting the knee during cycling); cartilage absorbs impact forces when landing from a jump; synovial fluid lubricates the joint and reduces the wear on cartilage surfaces during sustained aerobic exercise. Always name the structure, state what it does, and give a sporting example.
anchors.new: Rank ligaments, bursae, cartilage and synovial fluid by how much each protects a player landing from a jump. Defend each place in one line.

anchors.old: Without looking, write the full pathway of blood through the heart in order: start with 'deoxygenated blood enters...' and finish with 'oxygenated blood leaves via...'. Include all four chambers and all four major vessels.
anchors.text: Key Fact Blood pathway: vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs (gas exchange) → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body. Note that the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood — this is the opposite of most arteries.
anchors.new: Draw from memory a flow chart of blood from the vena cava to the aorta, then mark each stage as oxygenated or deoxygenated.

anchors.old: Cover this and calculate cardiac output for: (1) a resting heart rate of 72 bpm and stroke volume of 70 ml; (2) an exercising heart rate of 160 bpm and stroke volume of 100 ml. Show the formula, substitution and units.
anchors.text: Key Fact Cardiac output (Q) = stroke volume × heart rate. Always show the formula, substitute the values, and include the unit (ml/min or L/min). Example: Q = 70 ml × 72 bpm = 5,040 ml/min. At maximum exercise this can rise to over 20,000 ml/min in a trained athlete.
anchors.new: Predict whether Q at 200 bpm and a stroke volume of 110 ml beats 20,000 ml/min, then check it using the formula, the substitution and the unit.

anchors.text: Vasoconstriction and vasodilation: redirecting blood during exercise During exercise, the working muscles need much more oxygen and glucose than at rest. The body redirects blood flow using two mechanisms. Vasoconstriction reduces the diameter of blood vessels supplying areas that are not active during exercise (e.g. the digestive system), reducing blood flow to those areas. Vasodilation increases the diameter of the blood vessels supplying the active muscles, dramatically increasing blood flow to where it is needed most. The redistribution of blood during exercise through vasoconstriction and vasodilation is called the ‘vascular shunt’. This is why it is inadvisable to exercise vigorously immediately after a large meal — the digestive system is competing with muscles for blood supply.
anchors.new: Pick a sport you play and name the body areas where vasoconstriction and vasodilation would act during a match, then explain the vascular shunt.

food-preparation-and-nutrition-aqa/food-.title: Why Food is Cooked and Heat Transfer

anchors.old: Cover this and recall: what are the five reasons why food is cooked? Write each one in a single word before checking back.
anchors.text: Key Fact The five reasons food is cooked: make food safe; develop flavours; improve texture; improve shelf life; give variety in the diet. All five are expected in the written paper.
anchors.new: Choose a meal you ate this week and say which of the five reasons for cooking (safe, flavour, texture, shelf life, variety) applied to it, and how.

anchors.old: Without looking: name the three methods of heat transfer and give one cooking example for each. Then check your answers above.
anchors.text: Key Fact Conduction: heat passes through direct contact (frying pan to food). Convection: heat moves through circulating currents in liquid or gas (boiling water, oven air). Radiation: heat travels as infrared waves (grill browning a surface).
anchors.new: Sketch a frying pan, a pan of boiling water and a grill from memory, adding arrows to show conduction, convection and radiation at work in each.

anchors.text: Why does a white sauce need constant stirring? When you make a béchamel sauce, conduction heats the milk and roux from below, while convection currents try to circulate the liquid. However, starch granules can settle at the bottom and scorch before the top of the sauce even heats through. Stirring constantly does two things: it breaks up the convection pattern so all the sauce heats evenly, and it keeps the starch granules suspended so they don’t stick and burn. Without agitation, the starch at the bottom scorches while the top stays raw — you end up with a lumpy, bitter sauce. This is why the spec specifically lists “the need for agitation” when cooking a sauce.
anchors.new: Stop stirring a béchamel sauce for five minutes: say what happens to the starch granules, the convection currents and the final taste and texture.

anchors.old: Cover this and recall: what are the four functional properties of proteins? Then write one named food example for each one without looking.
anchors.text: Key Fact Four functional properties of proteins: denaturation (egg turns opaque in a hot pan); coagulation (quiche custard sets on baking); gluten formation (elastic dough develops when wheat flour is kneaded with water); foam formation (whisked egg whites trap air for a whisked sponge).
anchors.new: Choose a dish you eat at home and say which of denaturation, coagulation, gluten formation and foam formation happen in it, naming the step that causes each.

anchors.old: Cover this and recall: what happens to a starch granule as a sauce heats above 60 degrees C? Describe the three stages (swell, burst, thicken) before looking back.
anchors.text: Key Fact Gelatinisation: starch granules absorb liquid and swell above 60°C, burst around 85°C, releasing starch molecules that tangle and thicken the liquid. Starch-to-liquid ratio controls viscosity — more starch gives a thicker result.
anchors.new: Imagine a béchamel sauce is heated only to 65°C instead of 85°C. Say what happens to the starch granules and how thick the sauce ends up.

anchors.text: Misconception: denaturation and coagulation are the same thing Students frequently use these terms interchangeably, but they are two distinct stages. Denaturation is the unfolding of the protein’s shape — the bonds holding the coiled structure are broken and the protein becomes a loose chain. At this point the protein is still a separate molecule. Coagulation only happens afterwards: the loose, denatured chains start bonding to each other, forming a new cross-linked solid structure. So denaturation must happen first; coagulation is what follows. Think of it as “unravel, then re-join”. A 4-mark Explain question may specifically ask you to sequence these two stages — if you confuse them or call them the same process, you will lose marks.
anchors.new: Explain the difference between denaturation and coagulation to a Year 7, using your own everyday comparison instead of 'unravel, then re-join'.

food-preparation-and-nutrition-aqa/food-.title: Fats, Fruit & Vegetables and Raising Agents

anchors.old: Cover this and recall: name the four functional properties of fats and oils, and give one cooking example for each. Write them all before checking back.
anchors.text: Key Fact Four functional properties of fats and oils: shortening (pastry — fat coats flour, limits gluten); aeration (creamed cake — fat traps air with sugar); plasticity (croissant layers — fat works at a range of temperatures); emulsification (mayonnaise — egg yolk lecithin stabilises oil in water).
anchors.new: Say what would go wrong if croissants were made with a fat that lacks plasticity, first in a cold kitchen and then in a warm one.

anchors.old: Cover this and recall: what are the four types of raising agent? For each type, name one example and the gas it introduces. Check your answers.
anchors.text: Key Fact Four raising agents: chemical (baking powder, bicarbonate of soda, self-raising flour — produce CO⊂2;); mechanical (whisking, creaming, folding, sieving, rubbing in — incorporate air); steam (water in the mixture turns to steam at 100°C — expands and raises); biological (yeast produces CO⊂2; by fermentation — raises bread).
anchors.new: Pick a bake you like and say which raising agents it uses (chemical, mechanical, steam or biological) and how each one makes it rise.

anchors.text: Misconception: enzymic browning and oxidation are the same process Both involve oxygen, but they are different reactions. Enzymic browning is enzyme-driven: it requires the polyphenol oxidase enzyme released from damaged plant cells. You can stop enzymic browning by inactivating the enzyme (heat, acid, or lack of oxygen). Oxidation does not require an enzyme — it is a direct chemical reaction between vitamin C (or fats) and atmospheric oxygen. Storing cut vegetables in an airtight container slows oxidative vitamin C loss, but it will not prevent enzymic browning once the enzymes have been released. The distinction matters because the control methods differ: acid prevents enzymic browning but does not protect vitamin C from oxidative loss.
anchors.new: Argue for and against storing cut apple in an airtight container, using enzymic browning and vitamin C oxidation, then decide.
